gloss: Administrative: module 1 of a submission, the forms, labelling and correspondence.
Summaries: module 2, the overviews that condense the quality and study data.
Quality: module 3, how the substance and the product are made and tested.
Nonclinical: module 4, the laboratory and animal studies.
Clinical: module 5, the studies in people.
Half-life: the time the plasma concentration takes to fall by half.
Steady state: reached on repeated dosing, when intake and elimination balance.
Cmax: the highest plasma concentration reached after a dose.
Tmax: the time after a dose at which the plasma concentration peaks.
AUC: the area under the concentration–time curve, a measure of total exposure.
Bioavailability: the share of a dose that reaches the bloodstream unchanged.
First-pass: loss of a swallowed dose in the gut wall and liver before it circulates.
High-fat meal: the standard test of whether food changes a drug’s absorption.
Protein binding: the share of drug in plasma held by proteins and not free to act.
Volume of distribution: how far a drug spreads from plasma into the tissues.
Clearance: the volume of plasma freed of drug per unit of time.
Hepatic: of the liver, where most drugs are metabolized.
Renal: of the kidneys, which excrete drugs and metabolites in urine.
Metabolite: a compound the body makes from a drug; some are active themselves.
Prodrug: an inactive form that the body converts into the active drug.
CYP3A4: a liver enzyme that clears about half of all drugs.
CYP2D6: a liver enzyme whose activity differs widely from person to person.
CYP2C19: a liver enzyme with common genetic variants that slow or speed clearance.
CYP2C9: a liver enzyme that clears many acidic drugs; its activity varies by genotype.
P-gp: P-glycoprotein, a pump that carries drugs out of cells in the gut and elsewhere.
Salt: an ionic form of a drug, chosen for stability or solubility.
Free base: the drug molecule on its own, without the acid that makes it a salt.
Active moiety: the part of a substance that acts, leaving out its salt or ester.
Hydrate: a crystal form that holds water, one molecule in a monohydrate.
Enantiomer: one of the two mirror-image forms of a molecule; a racemate has both.
Monoclonal antibody: an antibody made by one cell line, so every copy is identical.
Isotype: the class of an antibody’s constant region, such as IgG1 or IgG4.
Expression system: the living cells engineered to produce a biologic.
kDa: kilodalton, a thousand daltons; the unit of mass used for proteins.
NDA: New Drug Application, the US marketing application for a chemical drug.
BLA: Biologics License Application, the US marketing application for a biologic.
Generic name: the nonproprietary name of the active substance, not a brand.
Boxed warning: the strongest warning on a US label, printed inside a black box.
Contraindication: a situation in which the drug must not be used.
Adverse reaction: an unwanted effect reasonably attributed to the drug.
Selectivity: how strongly a drug prefers its target over related ones.
Kinase: an enzyme that switches proteins on or off by adding phosphate.
Agonist: a drug that activates a receptor.
Antagonist: a drug that occupies a receptor without activating it.
